title: Count Set Bits
statement:
Count how many bits are set in an 8-bit value -- the same exercise as the
other *Count Set Bits* problems, in VHDL's own terms.

## Your entity

```
entity solution is
    port (
        value : in  std_logic_vector(7 downto 0);
        count : out std_logic_vector(3 downto 0)
    );
end entity solution;
```

`value` is the 8 bits to count; `count` is how many of them are `1`, wide
enough for every possible answer (0 to 8 fits in 4 bits). Port names and
widths must match exactly -- the testbench instantiates `solution` directly,
by name, rather than through a component declaration.

## Input and output

This is a circuit, not a program, so there is no `scanf`/`printf` here: the
testbench reads one line of stdin as an 8-character bit string, drives it
onto `value`, waits for the outputs to settle, and writes `count` back out
the same way -- also a bit string, left-padded with zeros to 4 characters.

`10110000` -> `0011` (three of the eight bits are set).

## Watch out

- This is meant to be pure combinational logic -- one concurrent signal
  assignment, or a process with `value` in its sensitivity list and no
  `wait` or clock inside it. Anything clocked has nothing to synchronise
  with here and will not have settled by the testbench's `wait for 1 ns`.
- `count` needs a value for every one of the 256 possible inputs. A process
  that only assigns it inside an `if` with no covering `else` leaves it
  latched at whatever it last held -- which behaves like a real latch in
  simulation, not just as a lint warning.

tests.name: all zero
tests.description: No bits set. Checks the all-else-branches-latch trap on the emptiest input.

tests.name: all ones
tests.description: Every bit set -- the one case where the 4-bit answer needs its own top bit.

tests.name: alternating
tests.description: Four bits set, spread out rather than adjacent.
